question.text: Does laparoscopic antireflux surgery improve quality of life in patients whose gastro-oesophageal reflux disease is well controlled with medical therapy?
question.context: Both medical therapy and laparoscopic antireflux surgery have been shown to improve quality of life in gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. Although patients with poor symptom control or side effects on medical therapy might be expected to have improved quality of life after surgery, our aim was to determine, for the first time, whether patients whose symptoms are well controlled on medical therapy but who decide to undergo surgery (patient preference) would experience improved quality of life. Retrospective analysis of our patient database (1998-2003, n=313) identified 60 patients who underwent laparoscopic antireflux surgery for the indication of patient preference. Two generic quality-of-life questionnaires (Short Form 36 and Psychological General Well-Being index) and a gastrointestinal symptom questionnaire (Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale) were completed preoperatively, while on medical therapy, and 6 months after surgery. Thirty-eight patients completed all three questionnaires at both time intervals: 31 males, seven females; mean age 42 (15-66) years. Preoperative scores while on medical therapy were significantly improved after surgery: Short Form 36 median physical composite scores 52.0 and 54.0 (P=0.034) and mental composite scores 51.0 and 56.0 (P=0.020); Psychological General Well-Being median total scores 78.0 and 90.0 (P=0.0001); Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale median total scores 2.13 and 1.73 (P=0.0007) and reflux scores 2.50 and 1.00 (P<0.0001).

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study found significant improvements in quality of life, including physical and mental health scores, psychological well-being, and gastrointestinal symptoms, in patients who underwent laparoscopic antireflux surgery after being well-controlled on medical therapy. This suggests that surgery can improve quality of life in this specific patient population.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Preoperative scores while on medical therapy were significantly improved after surgery: Short Form 36 median physical composite scores 52.0 and 54.0 (P=0.034) and mental composite scores 51.0 and 56.0 (P=0.020); Psychological General Well-Being median total scores 78.0 and 90.0 (P=0.0001); Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale median total scores 2.13 and 1.73 (P=0.0007) and reflux scores 2.50 and 1.00 (P<0.0001).
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While the study focuses on patients with well-controlled GERD, it's important to consider that other factors could influence quality of life. However, the significant improvements observed in the study strongly suggest that surgery is beneficial for this specific group of patients.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study shows that patients with well-controlled GERD who undergo laparoscopic antireflux surgery experience significant improvements in quality of life as measured by multiple validated questionnaires. The statistically significant improvements in both physical and mental composite scores (Short Form 36), psychological well-being (Psychological General Well-Being index), and gastrointestinal symptoms (Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale) strongly support the conclusion that surgery improves quality of life in this specific patient population.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The statistically significant improvements in both physical (P=0.034) and mental (P=0.020) Short Form 36 composite scores, along with the highly significant improvements in Psychological General Well-Being (P=0.0001) and Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale scores (P=0.0007 for total and P<0.0001 for reflux), provide compelling evidence that surgery improves quality of life in patients with well-controlled GERD who undergo the procedure.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: While patient preference and surgical risks were potential confounding factors, the study's retrospective design and large sample size (n=60) with complete data from 38 patients allowed for statistically significant comparisons. The focus on patients with well-controlled symptoms on medical therapy specifically addresses the question of whether surgery provides additional benefit beyond medical management.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study shows statistically significant improvements in multiple quality-of-life measures (physical, mental, psychological, and gastrointestinal symptom scores) after surgery in patients who were already well-controlled on medical therapy. This indicates that patient preference alone can lead to meaningful quality-of-life gains, even without symptom improvement.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Median Psychological General Well-Being scores improved from 78.0 to 90.0 (P=0.0001), and reflux scores dropped from 2.50 to 1.00 (P<0.0001), demonstrating substantial improvement despite preoperative medical control.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Differential diagnoses such as surgical failure or worsening symptoms were considered, but the data show consistent improvement across all measures, ruling out negative outcomes.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Other possibilities such as "C" (maybe) or "B" (no) are less supported because the data clearly shows positive changes post-surgery. Differential diagnoses such as unresponsive GERD or severe comorbidities were not mentioned, so the focus remains on the surgical outcome's impact on quality of life in this specific well-controlled group.
